summary: This standards-track memo specifies how to store in the DNS the mapping information (MCGAM) that MIXER-conformant gateways need to map RFC 822 domain names to X.400 O/R names and back.

plainLanguage.summary: Using the Internet phone book to also look up how to address a letter in the other mail system.

questions: what is the dns px record
how to map x400 addresses to rfc822
subtitle: How to publish X.400 and RFC 822 address mapping rules in the DNS instead of in hand-distributed tables.

tldr.problem: Gateways between Internet mail (RFC 822) and X.400 mail need tables that map domain names to X.400 O/R names and back. Keeping those tables identical on every gateway, and redistributing them after every change, is slow and laborious.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines one new DNS resource record, PX (type 26), plus a new branch of the name space labelled X42D under each country top-level domain. Mapping rules are written as ordinary DNS records, so gateways just query the DNS.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can publish their own mapping rules from their local DNS server without central coordination. The memo obsoletes RFC 1664 and is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 3597.

facts.label: Reserved label
facts.value: X42D, under each country top-level domain

today: RFC 2163 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1664, and it has been updated by RFC 3597.

sections.title: The Mapping Problem
sections.content:
MIXER describes how to convert addresses, envelopes and message bodies between X.400 mail and RFC 822 mail. Part of that job is a database that maps X.400 O/R addresses to RFC 822 domain names and back. In RFC 1327 this database was static: every gateway needed coherent copies of the same tables, and every update had to be distributed again.

MIXER replaces the idea of one global table with the MIXER Conformant Global Address Mapping (MCGAM). A gateway no longer has to know the complete set of rules, but the rules do need an efficient way to be published. MIXER proposes two: the Internet DNS and X.500. This memo is the full specification for the DNS method.

The memo obsoletes RFC 1664, which first proposed using the DNS with two new record types (TO-X400 and TO-822). This revision needs only one new record type and fully supports the new gate1 table, while keeping backward compatibility with RFC 1664.
sections.plainLanguage: Two groups write addresses in different styles, so mail needs a translator. The old way was a giant dictionary that everyone had to copy. This memo says to keep the translations where anyone can look them up.

sections.title: Why Use the DNS
sections.content:
The memo lists the advantages of a DNS-based system over a table-based one:

  • Hosts do not have to fetch and store entire mapping tables to run a MIXER gateway or tool.
  • Changes can be made available more quickly.
  • Authority can be fully delegated, in line with the Internet regionalization process.
  • Table management is not necessarily required for DNS-based gateways.
  • You can see the mappings a remote gateway is using by querying the DNS, which helps remote debugging.

Other tools, such as address converters and mail user agents, can also use the mapping rules in real time instead of carrying their own copy.
sections.plainLanguage: Looking a word up when you need it is easier than carrying a heavy dictionary everywhere. Updates also reach everybody at once.

sections.title: A Name Space for X.400 Addresses
sections.content:
MIXER mapping information is made of four tables. table1 and gate1 translate X.400 to RFC 822; table2 and gate2 translate RFC 822 to X.400. Each rule has the form keyword#translator#.

The keyword of a table2 or gate2 rule is already an RFC 822 domain, so it fits in the normal DNS tree. The keyword of a table1 or gate1 rule is an X.400 name, which needs a new structure. A single global branch, like in-addr.arpa, was considered but would have needed a central authority to coordinate every national X.400 name tree.

Instead, the memo places a reserved label X42D under each country top-level domain. The X.400 country codes are the same two-letter ISO codes the DNS uses for countries, so they make a natural hook. Below X42D the tree follows the X.400 hierarchy of ADMD, PRMD, O and OU. This moves the coordination problem to the national level, where the memo argues it is easier to solve.

Local mappings are not meant for use outside their own environment, so they should not be put in the DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: Every country already has its own two-letter code in the Internet phone book. Each country gets a special shelf labelled X42D for the other mail system's names, so no single world office has to run it.

sections.title: The PX Resource Record
sections.content:
The memo defines a new DNS resource record called PX (pointer to X.400/RFC 822 mapping information), class IN, type value 26. Its data has three parts: a 16-bit PREFERENCE (lower is preferred, as for MX), MAP822, which holds the RFC 822 part of the rule, and MAPX400, which holds the X.400 part written in DNS-compatible syntax. Both are domain-name elements, and PX records cause no additional section processing.

The owner name depends on the table. For table1 and gate1 entries it is an X.400 mail domain name in DNS syntax. For table2 and gate2 entries it is an RFC 822 mail domain. In the RDATA, the RFC 822 domain always comes before the X.400 part, even for table1 and gate1.

Every MCGAM rule is an implicit wildcard: a rule for net2.it covers any domain ending in net2.it unless a more specific rule exists. In the DNS, a name such as *.net2.it. gives that wildcard match, while a name without the asterisk matches exactly. The preference value and exact-match records are extensions that MIXER static tables cannot express, so the memo strongly discourages them when working with table-based gateways. For current use, the preference should be fixed at 50 and only wildcard names should be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The new kind of phone-book entry holds a pair: the address in one style and the same address in the other style. A star in the name means 'this and everything below it'.

sections.title: Writing X.400 Names as DNS Names
sections.content:
DNS labels allow only letters, digits and hyphens, but MIXER rules use the wider IA5 printable character set and $ separators. The memo defines a conversion. An attribute such as PRMD$ab becomes PRMD-ab; a missing value (O$@) becomes just the label (O); a blank value (ADMD$ ) becomes ADMDb.

Inside values, a hyphen becomes -h-, a quoted dot becomes -d-, a blank becomes -b-, and any other non-alphanumeric character becomes its three-digit decimal ASCII code between hyphens. A trailing hyphen produced by the translation is dropped. The string is parsed from left to right without revisiting text already translated, and the memo includes two flow charts for the conversion in each direction.

For the owner name of a table1 or gate1 record, the Country Code convention applies: the C-cc part is omitted and X42D.cc. is added instead, because the country code is identical to the top-level domain where the record lives.

Records for the gate1 and gate2 tables use the same rules, but the MAPX400 value ends with an extra .G.. That flag tells the gateway the answer is a gate entry, and it must be removed before the data is used. Because every X.400 domain ends in a country code, the flag cannot clash with real data.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone book only allows plain letters, digits and dashes. So odd characters get swapped for little codes, like writing 'dash' in words, and a tail tag marks entries for special gateways.

sections.title: Looking Up a Mapping
sections.content:
When a gateway needs a mapping, it asks the DNS for the PX record. The DNS itself returns the longest matching rule in a single query, so the iterative search through a table that MIXER describes is not needed. A search can succeed, fail, or, new with the DNS, time out. On timeout the gateway delays the operation and retries later; if the DNS returns an error code, an error message should be logged and the operation delayed in the same way.

The memo walks through four cases. For the RFC 822 name SUN.CCE.NRC.IT, a record at *.cce.nrc.it. returns a table2 rule. For a domain under MW, a record whose data ends in .G. returns a gate2 rule and tells the gateway to use DDA encoding. For an X.400 address with C=de; ADMD=pkz; PRMD=nfc; O=top, the gateway queries O-top.PRMD-nfc.ADMD-pkz.X42D.de. and the wildcard record at *.ADMD-pkz.X42D.de. answers with a table1 rule. A .G. record on the X.400 side marks a gate1 rule and means LHS encoding.

The authority that runs a domain decides how it is mapped. If it chooses Standard Attributes, it publishes a table entry; if it chooses DDAs (or LHS encoding on the X.400 side), it publishes a gate entry. A domain therefore never has both, and the gateway's action is clear.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail program asks the phone book once and gets the best matching answer. If the phone book does not answer in time, it simply tries again a bit later.

sections.title: Coexisting with Tables and X.500
sections.content:
Not every gateway will be able to use the DNS. The memo expects management domains to be table-based, DNS-based or X.500-based. Table-based domains keep publishing their rules through the International Mapping Table coordinator, and the DNS authorities can republish those rules the same way MX records are handled: if a branch has no DNS server of its own, a higher authority in the tree can serve it. A transition like the one from hosts.txt to DNS is suggested.

Keeping DNS and X.500 aligned is harder and needs some uploading between the two systems; the memo points to existing work on this. It also notes that MIXER no longer requires a gateway to know the complete set of rules. A gateway uses some set of valid rules, possibly incomplete or supplemented by local unpublished ones, so coordination between the three publication methods matters for efficiency, not for correct behaviour.
sections.plainLanguage: Some towns will keep using the paper book, some the phone book and some another directory. That is fine, because nobody needs every page to do their own job.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
PX records steer how addresses are translated between X.400 and Internet mail, so an attack on them can affect mail routing. A successful attack could forge an originator address, misdirect mail to an unauthorized recipient, make a message appear to be intended for other recipients, or force the mail through a gateway or message transfer agent running compromised software.

The memo names three ways incorrect PX records could reach a client: compromise of a DNS server, a counterfeit response to a query, and incorrect additional information returned for an unrelated query. Clients SHOULD base routing and address translation only on authoritative answers. Once the DNS security mechanisms of RFC 2065 become more widely deployed, clients SHOULD use them to verify the authenticity and integrity of PX records.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone sneaks a fake entry into the phone book, letters could go to the wrong house. So you should only trust answers from the real owner and check they are genuine.
